idea: A line drawing of Harrison's H4 sea watch (drawn in code, or from an archive engraving) with the caption 'Lost 5 seconds in 81 days.' On its 1761-62 trial voyage to Jamaica the watch solved longitude, and the shirt is for people who love precision.

An engraved square-rigger under full sail with Beaufort's scale as a column of words beside it, ending 'Force 12: No canvas could withstand.' Beaufort's 1805 scale was first defined by what a ship's sails could carry.

A Haeckel Kunstformen jellyfish (Discomedusae) plate with the caption 'No brain. Over 500 million years. Fine.' Jellyfish fossils go back more than 500 million years, and the shirt is a dry argument for doing less.
A crop of a sea monster from Olaus Magnus's 1539 Carta Marina with the caption 'Not a monster. A whale, mostly.' It is a point of view about how we draw what we cannot see.

A tide curve drawn in code as the sum of several sine waves, each labelled with its cause (M2 'Moon', S2 'Sun', K1 'Moon and Sun's tilt'), with the caption 'The sea, added up.' Lord Kelvin's tide-predicting machine of 1872 did the same sum with pulleys and wire.

An engraved cross-section of a Fresnel lighthouse lens with the caption 'A lamp, made brighter by arranging glass.' Fresnel's lens first went into the Cordouan lighthouse in 1823, and it is a love letter to optics.

A line engraving of the warship Vasa with the caption 'Maiden voyage. About 1,300 metres. Raised 1961.' The Vasa sank in Stockholm harbour in 1628 and was salvaged in 1961. It is for people who respect ambitious failure.

Franklin and Folger's 1769-70 Gulf Stream chart, with the caption 'Mapped by a postmaster, from whalers' knowledge.' Franklin got the data from his Nantucket whaling cousin Timothy Folger, and it is a shirt about listening to people who do the work.

Three whale silhouettes from public-domain plates labelled 'Folio', 'Octavo' and 'Duodecimo', captioned 'Whales, by book size. H. Melville, 1851.' Melville's Cetology chapter really sorts whales this way, and it is for readers.
An old rigging-manual engraving of a bowline knot with the caption 'Holds the whole load. Still unties.' The bowline does not slip or jam, and it is a quiet shirt about being reliable.

A portolan-style compass rose with the eight Mediterranean winds named at its points: Tramontana, Greco, Levante, Scirocco, Ostro, Libeccio, Ponente, Maestro. Typographic, beautiful, and the wind names are real.

Luke Howard's engraved cloud studies (cirrus, cumulus, stratus) with the caption 'Named in 1802 by a pharmacist.' Howard was a pharmacist and gave clouds the Latin names we still use, and the shirt is for sky-watchers.

A chambered nautilus cross-section drawn in code as a logarithmic spiral, with the line 'Build thee more stately mansions.' It is from Oliver Wendell Holmes's 1858 poem about the nautilus, and it is a gift for the quietly ambitious.

An engraving of the barnacle goose tree from Gerard's 1597 Herball, with geese hatching from barnacles and the caption 'Barnacles once thought to hatch geese.' It is a shirt about confident wrong ideas, with the true origin of the name.

A sounding line, lead weight and rope drawn as an engraving with the caption 'How deep? Rope and lead.' The Challenger expedition of 1872-76 sounded the deep ocean with exactly that, and the shirt is for the stubbornly curious.

An engraved argonaut (paper nautilus) with the caption 'Aristotle thought it sailed. It's an egg case.' The shell is a brood chamber made by the female, and the shirt is for fans of lovely corrections.

A crop of Mercator's 1569 world map showing Greenland beside Africa, with the caption 'Made so a compass bearing is a straight line. Greenland is not that big.' Africa is about 14 times larger, and it is a shirt about useful distortions.

An engraved Eddystone lighthouse by Smeaton with the caption 'Smeaton, 1759. Modelled on an oak trunk.' Smeaton said he took the curve from an oak, dovetailed the granite blocks, and the tower stood for over a century.
A seahorse from an old natural-history engraving with the caption 'The father carries the young.' Male seahorses brood the eggs in a pouch, and it is a warm, true, slightly subversive shirt.

Gustave Doré's 1876 albatross from The Rime of the Ancient Mariner with the caption 'Crossbow, 1798. Bad idea.' It nods to Coleridge, and a wandering albatross has a wingspan of about 3.5 metres, for those who like literary jokes.
